listen_text: Example: the language of arithmetic has one binary less-than predicate, constant zero, unary successor, and binary addition and multiplication functions.
long_description: The example identifies the nonlogical vocabulary used for arithmetic.
ordered_steps: Example: the language of arithmetic has one binary less-than predicate, constant zero, unary successor, and binary addition and multiplication functions.

listen_text: Example: the language of set theory contains only the binary membership predicate.
long_description: The example identifies the sole nonlogical symbol of the set-theory language.
ordered_steps: Example: the language of set theory contains only the binary membership predicate.

listen_text: Example: the language of orders contains only the binary less-than-or-equal-to predicate.
long_description: The example identifies the sole nonlogical symbol of the language of orders.
ordered_steps: Example: the language of orders contains only the binary less-than-or-equal-to predicate.

listen_text: Definition of terms: every variable is a term; every language constant is a term; and applying an n-place function to n terms produces a term. Nothing else is a term. A term with no variables is closed.
long_description: The definition gives every formation clause for terms and excludes all other strings.
ordered_steps: Definition of terms: every variable is a term; every language constant is a term; and applying an n-place function to n terms produces a term. Nothing else is a term. A term with no variables is closed.

listen_text: Definition of formulas: falsum and truth, when present, are atomic formulas. An n-place predicate applied to n terms is atomic, and identity between two terms is atomic. Negation preserves formula status. Applying a binary connective to two formulas produces a formula. Universal or existential quantification of a formula by a variable produces a formula. Nothing else is a formula.
long_description: The definition gives the atomic, connective, and quantifier formation clauses and the limiting clause.
ordered_steps: Definition of formulas: falsum and truth, when present, are atomic formulas. An n-place predicate applied to n terms is atomic, and identity between two terms is atomic. Negation preserves formula status. Applying a binary connective to two formulas produces a formula. Universal or existential quantification of a formula by a variable produces a formula. Nothing else is a formula.

listen_text: Defined operators are abbreviations. In this profile, truth abbreviates not falsum, and A if and only if B abbreviates the conjunction of if A then B and if B then A. These abbreviations do not add primitive symbols.
long_description: The active first-order profile displays exactly the definitions of truth and the biconditional.
ordered_steps: Defined operators are abbreviations. In this profile, truth abbreviates not falsum, and A if and only if B abbreviates the conjunction of if A then B and if B then A. These abbreviations do not add primitive symbols.

listen_text: Definition: A is syntactically identical to B exactly when A and B have the same length and the same symbol at every position.
long_description: The definition distinguishes exact string identity from truth-functional or semantic equivalence.
ordered_steps: Definition: A is syntactically identical to B exactly when A and B have the same length and the same symbol at every position.

listen_text: Lemma: let L be a first-order language. If property P holds for every variable, every constant of L, and every function term whenever it holds for all argument terms, then P holds for every term of L.
long_description: The lemma states the structural induction principle for first-order terms.
ordered_steps: Lemma: let L be a first-order language. If property P holds for every variable, every constant of L, and every function term whenever it holds for all argument terms, then P holds for every term of L.

listen_text: Exercise: prove the principle of induction on terms stated immediately before this exercise. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for the proof of the preceding term-induction lemma.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove the principle of induction on terms stated immediately before this exercise. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Lemma: if property P holds for all atomic formulas and is preserved by every configured unary, binary, universal, and existential formation clause, then P holds for every formula of language L.
long_description: The lemma states structural induction over atomic, connective, and quantified formulas.
ordered_steps: Lemma: if property P holds for all atomic formulas and is preserved by every configured unary, binary, universal, and existential formation clause, then P holds for every formula of language L.

listen_text: Lemma: the number of left parentheses in any formula A equals the number of right parentheses in A.
long_description: The lemma says each formula has equally many opening and closing parentheses.
ordered_steps: Lemma: the number of left parentheses in any formula A equals the number of right parentheses in A.

listen_text: Exercise: prove that every term t has equally many left and right parentheses. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for the corresponding balanced-parentheses result for terms.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove that every term t has equally many left and right parentheses. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Definition: string B is a proper prefix of string A when appending a nonempty string of symbols to B yields A.
long_description: The definition says how one symbol string can be an initial but incomplete part of another.
ordered_steps: Definition: string B is a proper prefix of string A when appending a nonempty string of symbols to B yields A.

listen_text: Lemma: if A is a formula and B is a proper prefix of A, then B is not a formula.
long_description: The lemma excludes a formula from being a proper prefix of another formula.
ordered_steps: Lemma: if A is a formula and B is a proper prefix of A, then B is not a formula.

listen_text: Exercise: prove that no proper prefix of a formula is itself a formula. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for a proof of the preceding lemma.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove that no proper prefix of a formula is itself a formula. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Proposition: every atomic formula has exactly one form: a configured truth or falsity constant, a predicate applied to uniquely determined terms, or identity between two uniquely determined terms.
long_description: The proposition classifies every atomic formula into exactly one atomic formation case.
ordered_steps: Proposition: every atomic formula has exactly one form: a configured truth or falsity constant, a predicate applied to uniquely determined terms, or identity between two uniquely determined terms.

listen_text: Exercise: prove the unique classification of atomic formulas. Hint: formulate and prove for terms a version of the no-proper-prefix lemma. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for the unique-atomic-form proof and suggests a term-prefix lemma.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove the unique classification of atomic formulas. Hint: formulate and prove for terms a version of the no-proper-prefix lemma. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Proposition: every formula has exactly one outer form: atomic, a negation, a configured binary connective applied to two formulas, a universal formula, or an existential formula. In each non-atomic case the immediate component formula or formulas are uniquely determined.
long_description: The proposition gives the exhaustive and mutually exclusive outer forms of a formula.
ordered_steps: Proposition: every formula has exactly one outer form: atomic, a negation, a configured binary connective applied to two formulas, a universal formula, or an existential formula. In each non-atomic case the immediate component formula or formulas are uniquely determined.

accessible_name: Definition of a formula's main operator
listen_text: Definition: an atomic formula has no main operator. A negation's main operator is its negation sign. A binary formula's main operator is its displayed binary connective. A universal or existential formula's main operator is its displayed quantifier occurrence.
long_description: The definition identifies the final and outermost operator used to construct a non-atomic formula.
ordered_steps: Definition: an atomic formula has no main operator. A negation's main operator is its negation sign. A binary formula's main operator is its displayed binary connective. A universal or existential formula's main operator is its displayed quantifier occurrence.

accessible_name: Table of main operators and formula types
listen_text: Table: atomic formulas have no main operator. Negation has the negation sign. Conjunction has and. Disjunction has or. A conditional has if-then. A biconditional has if-and-only-if. A universal formula has the universal quantifier. An existential formula has the existential quantifier. Each row includes the corresponding formula pattern.
long_description: The table pairs each outer operator with its formula type and an example.
ordered_steps: Table: atomic formulas have no main operator. Negation has the negation sign. Conjunction has and. Disjunction has or. A conditional has if-then. A biconditional has if-and-only-if. A universal formula has the universal quantifier. An existential formula has the existential quantifier. Each row includes the corresponding formula pattern.

listen_text: Definition: atomic formulas have no immediate subformulas. The immediate subformula of a negation or quantified formula is its scope. The immediate subformulas of a binary formula are its left and right component formulas.
long_description: The definition lists the direct formula components of every outer form.
ordered_steps: Definition: atomic formulas have no immediate subformulas. The immediate subformula of a negation or quantified formula is its scope. The immediate subformulas of a binary formula are its left and right component formulas.

listen_text: Definition: atomic formulas have no proper subformulas. For a negation or quantified formula, the proper subformulas are its scope and every proper subformula of that scope. For a binary formula, they are both components and every proper subformula of either component.
long_description: The recursive definition collects each immediate component and all of that component's proper subformulas.
ordered_steps: Definition: atomic formulas have no proper subformulas. For a negation or quantified formula, the proper subformulas are its scope and every proper subformula of that scope. For a binary formula, they are both components and every proper subformula of either component.

listen_text: Definition: the subformulas of A are A itself together with every proper subformula of A.
long_description: The definition adds a formula itself to all its proper subformulas.
ordered_steps: Definition: the subformulas of A are A itself together with every proper subformula of A.

listen_text: Proposition: if B is a subformula of A and C is a subformula of B, then C is a subformula of A.
long_description: The proposition states that a subformula of a subformula is a subformula of the original formula.
ordered_steps: Proposition: if B is a subformula of A and C is a subformula of B, then C is a subformula of A.

listen_text: Exercise: prove that the subformula relation is transitive. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for a proof of the preceding proposition.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove that the subformula relation is transitive. No solution is supplied here.

accessible_name: Upper bound on the number of subformulas
listen_text: Proposition: if formula A has n connectives and quantifiers, then A has at most two times n plus one subformulas.
long_description: The proposition bounds the number of subformulas using the count of connectives and quantifiers.
ordered_steps: Proposition: if formula A has n connectives and quantifiers, then A has at most two times n plus one subformulas.

listen_text: Exercise: prove that a formula with n connectives and quantifiers has at most two times n plus one subformulas. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for a proof of the preceding upper bound.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove that a formula with n connectives and quantifiers has at most two times n plus one subformulas. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Definition: if L is a first-order language, an L-string is a finite sequence of symbols of L. When L is fixed by context, it may simply be called a string.
long_description: The definition treats a string as a finite sequence of symbols of a fixed first-order language.
ordered_steps: Definition: if L is a first-order language, an L-string is a finite sequence of symbols of L. When L is fixed by context, it may simply be called a string.

accessible_name: Example of a string that is not a formula
listen_text: Example: every formula of language L is an L-string, but the converse fails. The displayed sequence closing parenthesis, opening parenthesis, v sub zero, conditional, existential quantifier is an L-string but not an L-formula.
long_description: The example distinguishes arbitrary language strings from well-formed formulas.
ordered_steps: Example: every formula of language L is an L-string, but the converse fails. The displayed sequence closing parenthesis, opening parenthesis, v sub zero, conditional, existential quantifier is an L-string but not an L-formula.

listen_text: Definition: a sequence from t sub zero through t sub n is a formation sequence for t when t is syntactically identical to t sub n and every entry is a variable, a constant, or a function application whose argument terms occur at earlier indices. Reader note: the source calls the displayed function k-ary but indexes its arguments from zero through k, displaying k plus one argument positions. The reader preserves that mismatch.
long_description: The definition characterizes a term by a finite sequence whose entries are variables, constants, or function terms built from earlier entries; a reader note flags the source's arity-versus-indexing mismatch.
ordered_steps: Definition: a sequence from t sub zero through t sub n is a formation sequence for t when t is syntactically identical to t sub n and every entry is a variable, a constant, or a function application whose argument terms occur at earlier indices. Reader note: the source calls the displayed function k-ary but indexes its arguments from zero through k, displaying k plus one argument positions. The reader preserves that mismatch.

listen_text: Example: the displayed sequences construct c sub zero and v sub zero, then apply the first binary function, then apply the first unary function to that term. Swapping the first two independent entries gives another valid formation sequence for the same final term.
long_description: The examples give two valid orders for constructing the same compound term.
ordered_steps: Example: the displayed sequences construct c sub zero and v sub zero, then apply the first binary function, then apply the first unary function to that term. Swapping the first two independent entries gives another valid formation sequence for the same final term.

listen_text: Definition: a sequence from A sub zero through A sub n is a formation sequence for A when A is syntactically identical to A sub n and every entry is atomic or is obtained from earlier entries by a configured negation, binary connective, universal quantifier, or existential quantifier clause.
long_description: The definition characterizes a formula by a finite sequence whose entries are atomic or built from earlier formulas.
ordered_steps: Definition: a sequence from A sub zero through A sub n is a formation sequence for A when A is syntactically identical to A sub n and every entry is atomic or is obtained from earlier entries by a configured negation, binary connective, universal quantifier, or existential quantifier clause.

listen_text: Example: one sequence constructs two atoms, their conjunction, and the existential quantification of that conjunction. A second valid sequence repeats an atom and includes an unused universal formula before reaching the same final existential formula.
long_description: The examples construct the same existential conjunction and show that redundant entries are permitted.
ordered_steps: Example: one sequence constructs two atoms, their conjunction, and the existential quantification of that conjunction. A second valid sequence repeats an atom and includes an unused universal formula before reaching the same final existential formula.

listen_text: Displayed sequence: an atom using v sub zero; an atom using c sub one; their conjunction; the c sub one atom again; an unused universal formula; and finally the existential quantification of the conjunction.
long_description: The display is the longer formation sequence from the preceding example.
ordered_steps: Displayed sequence: an atom using v sub zero; an atom using c sub one; their conjunction; the c sub one atom again; an unused universal formula; and finally the existential quantification of the conjunction.

listen_text: Proposition: every formula A in the set of formulas of language L has a formula formation sequence.
long_description: The proposition says every inductively well-formed formula has a formation sequence.
ordered_steps: Proposition: every formula A in the set of formulas of language L has a formula formation sequence.

listen_text: Lemma: if the sequence from A sub zero through A sub n is a formation sequence for A sub n and k is at most n, then the sequence from A sub zero through A sub k is a formation sequence for A sub k.
long_description: The lemma says an initial segment of a formation sequence is a formation sequence for its own final entry.
ordered_steps: Lemma: if the sequence from A sub zero through A sub n is a formation sequence for A sub n and k is at most n, then the sequence from A sub zero through A sub k is a formation sequence for A sub k.

listen_text: Exercise: prove the initial-subsequence lemma for formation sequences. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for a proof of the preceding lemma.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove the initial-subsequence lemma for formation sequences. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Theorem: the set of formulas of language L is exactly the set of L-strings for which a formula formation sequence exists.
long_description: The theorem equates inductively generated formulas with strings possessing formula formation sequences.
ordered_steps: Theorem: the set of formulas of language L is exactly the set of L-strings for which a formula formation sequence exists.

listen_text: Proposition: the set of terms of language L is exactly the set of L-strings for which a term formation sequence exists.
long_description: The proposition gives the analogous characterization of terms.
ordered_steps: Proposition: the set of terms of language L is exactly the set of L-strings for which a term formation sequence exists.

listen_text: Exercise: prove the formation-sequence characterization of terms, using a strategy like the preceding formula theorem. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for the term equivalence proof and points to the formula proof strategy.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove the formation-sequence characterization of terms, using a strategy like the preceding formula theorem. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Definition: a formation sequence ending at index n is minimal when every other formation sequence for the same formula or term has length at least n plus one.
long_description: The definition compares the length of a formation sequence with every other formation sequence for the same formula or term.
ordered_steps: Definition: a formation sequence ending at index n is minimal when every other formation sequence for the same formula or term has length at least n plus one.

listen_text: Proposition: B is a subformula of A exactly when B occurs in every formation sequence of A, and exactly when B occurs in a minimal formation sequence of A.
long_description: The proposition gives three equivalent ways to identify a subformula.
ordered_steps: Proposition: B is a subformula of A exactly when B occurs in every formation sequence of A, and exactly when B occurs in a minimal formation sequence of A.

accessible_name: Exercise on subformulas and formation sequences
listen_text: Exercise: prove the equivalence between being a subformula and occurring in every or in a minimal formation sequence. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for a proof of the preceding equivalence.
ordered_steps: Exercise: prove the equivalence between being a subformula and occurring in every or in a minimal formation sequence. No solution is supplied here.

listen_text: Definition: every variable occurrence in an atomic formula is free. Negation preserves the free occurrences of its component. A binary formula has the free occurrences from both components. Universal or existential quantification removes the bound variable's occurrences from the free occurrences of its scope.
long_description: The inductive definition tracks free occurrences through atomic, connective, and quantifier forms.
ordered_steps: Definition: every variable occurrence in an atomic formula is free. Negation preserves the free occurrences of its component. A binary formula has the free occurrences from both components. Universal or existential quantification removes the bound variable's occurrences from the free occurrences of its scope.

listen_text: Definition: a variable occurrence in formula A is bound exactly when it is not free.
long_description: The definition makes bound occurrence the complement of free occurrence within a formula.
ordered_steps: Definition: a variable occurrence in formula A is bound exactly when it is not free.

listen_text: Exercise: give an inductive definition of bound variable occurrences parallel to the definition of free occurrences. No solution is supplied here.
long_description: The exercise asks for a direct inductive definition of bound occurrences.
ordered_steps: Exercise: give an inductive definition of bound variable occurrences parallel to the definition of free occurrences. No solution is supplied here.

accessible_name: Definition of quantifier scope and binding
listen_text: Definition: in a quantified subformula, the corresponding occurrence of the quantified formula is the scope of that quantifier occurrence. Free occurrences of the quantified variable inside that scope become bound by the quantifier.
long_description: The definition identifies a quantifier's corresponding subformula occurrence and which free variable occurrences it binds.
ordered_steps: Definition: in a quantified subformula, the corresponding occurrence of the quantified formula is the scope of that quantifier occurrence. Free occurrences of the quantified variable inside that scope become bound by the quantifier.

accessible_name: Examples of scope, binding, and free variables
listen_text: Example: in the first existential formula, v sub zero is bound and v sub one remains free. In the larger formula, the main operator is a conditional. Its antecedent is the complete universal formula for every v sub zero, B, where B is that quantifier's conditional scope. Its consequent is the complete existential formula there exists v sub one, C, where C is that quantifier's disjunctive scope. D marks the negated-atom scope of the inner universal quantifier.
long_description: The examples trace bound and free occurrences through a simple existential and a nested compound formula.
ordered_steps: Example: in the first existential formula, v sub zero is bound and v sub one remains free. In the larger formula, the main operator is a conditional. Its antecedent is the complete universal formula for every v sub zero, B, where B is that quantifier's conditional scope. Its consequent is the complete existential formula there exists v sub one, C, where C is that quantifier's disjunctive scope. D marks the negated-atom scope of the inner universal quantifier.

listen_text: Definition: a formula A is a sentence exactly when it contains no free occurrences of variables.
long_description: The definition characterizes sentences by the absence of free variable occurrences.
ordered_steps: Definition: a formula A is a sentence exactly when it contains no free occurrences of variables.

accessible_name: Recursive definition of substitution in a term
listen_text: Definition: substituting t for x leaves a constant unchanged; leaves a variable y unchanged when y differs from x; replaces x by t; and recursively substitutes in every argument of a function term.
long_description: The definition gives the constant, distinct-variable, target-variable, and function-term cases.
ordered_steps: Definition: substituting t for x leaves a constant unchanged; leaves a variable y unchanged when y differs from x; replaces x by t; and recursively substitutes in every argument of a function term.

accessible_name: Definition of a term being free for a variable
listen_text: Definition: term t is free for x in formula A when no free occurrence of x in A lies within the scope of a quantifier that binds a variable occurring in t.
long_description: The definition states the capture-avoidance condition for formula substitution.
ordered_steps: Definition: term t is free for x in formula A when no free occurrence of x in A lies within the scope of a quantifier that binds a variable occurring in t.

accessible_name: Examples of terms free and not free for substitution
listen_text: Example: variable v sub eight is free for v sub one in the displayed existential atom. The binary term in v sub one and v sub two is not free for v sub zero in the displayed universal atom because the quantifier for v sub two would capture an occurrence.
long_description: The examples contrast a safe substitution term with one that would be captured.
ordered_steps: Example: variable v sub eight is free for v sub one in the displayed existential atom. The binary term in v sub one and v sub two is not free for v sub zero in the displayed universal atom because the quantifier for v sub two would capture an occurrence.

accessible_name: Recursive definition of substitution in a formula
listen_text: Definition: substitution leaves configured truth constants unchanged; recursively substitutes in every term of predicate and identity atoms; distributes through negation and each binary connective; and proceeds beneath a quantifier for y only when y differs from x, otherwise leaving that quantified formula unchanged. The term must be free for x in A.
long_description: The definition distributes capture-avoiding substitution through every atomic, connective, and quantifier form.
ordered_steps: Definition: substitution leaves configured truth constants unchanged; recursively substitutes in every term of predicate and identity atoms; distributes through negation and each binary connective; and proceeds beneath a quantifier for y only when y differs from x, otherwise leaving that quantified formula unchanged. The term must be free for x in A.
